human_tolerance.notes: Tolerant of human proximity to the point of thriving in crowded urban and suburban neighbourhoods, taking food and nest sites from human habitations and nesting in an attic as happily as in a hollow tree.

phases.name: breeding
phases.note: The earliest litters appear in late January and most births occur in mid-March and again in July; gestation runs 44 to 45 days and the average litter is three.

phases.name: caching
phases.note: Autumn food is acorns, hickory nuts, beechnuts, walnuts and butternuts; the squirrel buries caches of shelled, high-fat food for the winter, and juveniles disperse in September or October.

vocalizations.description: A series of barks; the most common vocalization of the species.
Tooth chatters and breathy barks, given when the animal is stressed. Grunts and squeals are also given by restrained animals and during male-male chases.

external.note: GBIF usage key and ITIS TSN read directly from the two databases; the iNaturalist taxon id via Wikidata (P3151).

conservation.note: Wikidata P141 = least concern (Q211005). The article's note that many subspecies are threatened refers to localized subspecies, not the species.

range.note: 'The fox squirrel's natural range extends through most of the eastern United States, north into the southern prairie provinces of Canada, west to the Dakotas, Colorado, and Texas, and south to the northern parts of Coahuila, Nuevo Leon and Tamaulipas.'

traits.locomotion_modes.note: 'however, agile climbers', with 'Fox squirrels are impressive jumpers, easily spanning 15 feet in horizontal leaps and free-falling 20 feet or more to a soft landing on a tree limb or tree trunk', and 'Fox squirrels are often observed foraging on the ground several hundred meters from the nearest woodlot'.

traits.flight.note: A ground-and-tree rodent with no wings and no gliding structure; 'None' follows from the description and from the wingless body plan.

traits.nest_type.note: 'Tree dens are preferred over leaf nests during the winter and for raising young. When den trees are scarce, leaf nests are used year-round.' Dens are hollowed tree trunks, so 'Cavity' is the matching nest type; the leafy summer dreys are the alternative the note records.

traits.perching.note: False: the species climbs trunks and leaps between branches but is not a perching bird and the quadruped body plan has no perched pose.

traits.mass_kg.note: Midpoint of 'They range in weight from 1.0 to 2.5 lb (453.6 to 1,134.0 g)'.

traits.length_m.note: Midpoint of total length, '20 to 30 in (50.8 to 76.2 cm)'.

traits.shoulder_height_m.note: Judgement: no open source gives a standing shoulder height for this species. Taken as about a third of the sourced 63.5 cm nose-to-tail length, which suits a low, flat-running ground squirrel; the same article's hind-foot length of 5.1-8.2 cm supports that scale.

traits.lifespan_y.note: 'Their maximum life expectancy is typically 12.6 years for females and 8.6 years for males'; 10.6 years is the midpoint of those two maxima, since the record carries a single lifespan field. The article separately notes that captive squirrels 'have been known to live about 18 years'.

traits.diet.note: Mast dominates: 'Autumn foods consist mainly of acorns, hickory nuts, beechnuts, walnuts, butternuts, and hazelnuts', with 'Spring foods are mainly tree buds and flowers, insects, bird eggs, and seeds'; agricultural crops and fruit are also eaten. Shares are a judgement.

traits.social.note: 'Fox squirrels are strictly diurnal, non-territorial', yet 'Cohabitation of these dens is not uncommon, particularly among breeding pairs'; a group size of one to two reflects den-sharing rather than a flock.

traits.activity_pattern.note: 'Fox squirrels are strictly diurnal, non-territorial, and spend more of their time on the ground than most other tree squirrels.'

traits.defense.note: The article's predator list runs from bobcats and coyotes down to snakes, and 'relatively few natural predators can regularly capture adult fox squirrels'; the response to a threat is to run or to retreat up a tree and bark, not to fight.

traits.wariness.note: 'Fox squirrels are tolerant of human proximity, and even thrive in crowded urban and suburban environments.'

habitat.use.note: 'spend more of their time on the ground than most other tree squirrels' while also nesting in tree dens high in branches; a near-even split is a judgement from that, not a stated figure.

habitat.shelter_tag.note: 'winter dens are usually hollowed out of tree trunks'; 'cavity' is the matching drawable shelter tag.

habitat.resources.note: Mast and seed diet, tree-cavity dens, leafy summer dreys and ground foraging under mature trees; weights are judgement.

habitat.human_tolerance.note: 'Fox squirrels are tolerant of human proximity, and even thrive in crowded urban and suburban environments. They exploit human habitations for sources of food and nesting sites, being as happy nesting in an attic as they are in a hollow tree.'

seasonal.strategy.note: A year-round resident that caches food rather than migrating or hibernating; no migration or hibernation is described anywhere in the article.

seasonal.winter_fraction.note: Follows from year-round residence: it den in the same tree through the winter.

seasonal.phases.note: 'The earliest litters appear in late January; most births occur in mid-March and July', with autumn mast and caching pressure from September; the exact windows here are a judgement placed on those statements.

seasonal.life_stages.note: 'Fox squirrels are weaned between 12 and 14 weeks, but may not be self-supporting until 16 weeks'; 98 days is the midpoint of the sourced weaning range, and the 0.7 scale is a judgement.

vocalizations.bark.note: 'The most common vocalization for fox squirrels is a series of barks.'

vocalizations.chatter.note: 'Tooth chatters and breathy barks are indications of stress. Grunts and squeals are given by restrained animals and during male-male chase.'

look.note: 'the animal's upper body is brown-grey to brown-yellow with a typically brownish-orange underside', with darker, more strongly patterned animals in the eastern mountains and a large bushy tail of similar length to the body; palette, proportions and box placement are judgement.

behavior.note: The shared fsm-ground-forager-v1 program fits a foraging rodent that eats from the landscape, caches, drinks and retreats to a den; food_tag is set to mast because nuts dominate the diet. rest_sun_lo_deg and rest_sun_hi_deg are set to -90 and -6 because the species is strictly diurnal, so it rests when the sun is down rather than during the day as the defaults assume.
